{{Use British English|date=June 2017}}
'''Colin Rourke''' (1 January 1943 &ndash; 18 December 2024) was a British mathematician who worked in [[Piecewise linear manifold|PL topology]], [[low-dimensional topology]], [[differential topology]], [[group theory]], [[Theory of relativity|relativity]] and [[cosmology]]. He was an emeritus professor at the Mathematics Institute at the [[University of Warwick]] and a founding editor of the journals ''[[Geometry & Topology]]'' and ''[[Algebraic & Geometric Topology]]'', published by [[Mathematical Sciences Publishers]], where he was a permanent member of its board of directors.<ref name=msp>{{cite web|title=Board of Directors|publisher=Mathematical Sciences Publishers|access-date=8 October 2015|url=http://msp.org/about/board/}}</ref>

== Career ==
Rourke obtained his [[PhD]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1965 under the direction of [[Christopher Zeeman]].<ref>{{MathGenealogyProject|24425}}</ref> Most of his early work was carried out in collaboration with Brian Sanderson. They solved a number of outstanding problems: the provision of [[normal bundle]]s for the PL category (which they called "Block bundles")<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rourke|first=C.P.|last2=Sanderson|first2=B.J.|title=Block Bundles I, II and III|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume=87 |issue=1968|pages=1–28, 255–277, 431–483|doi=10.2307/1970591 }}</ref>, and the non-existence of normal [[microbundle]]s (top and PL)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rourke|first=C.P.|last2=Sanderson|first2=B.J.|title=An embedding without a normal microbundle|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|volume=3 |issue=1967|pages=293–299}}</ref>. In collaboration with Sandro Buoncristiano, he  geometric interpretation for all (generalized) [[homology theories]]<ref>{{cite book|author1-last=Buoncristiano|author1-first=S.|author2-last=Rourke|author2-first=C. P.|author3-last=Sanderson|author3-first=B. J|title=A geometric approach to homology theory|url=https://archive.org/details/geometricapproac0000buon|url-access=registration|series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series|volume= 18|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=1976}}</ref>.

Rourke was an [[List of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker]] at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1970 at [[Nice]].<ref>{{cite web|publisher=International Mathematical Union|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897|url=http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|access-date=11 October 2015|archive-date=24 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171124141541/http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Rourke|first=C. P.|chapter=Block structures in geometric and algebraic topology|title=Actes du Congrès International des Mathématiciens (Nice, 1970)|volume=Tome 2|pages=127&ndash;32|publisher=Gauthier-Villars|location=Paris|year=1971}}</ref> From 1976 to 1981, he was acting professor of pure mathematics at the [[Open University]] (on secondment from Warwick) where he oversaw the rewriting of the pure mathematics course.

Rourke died in 2024, aged 81.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/general/news/new/in_memoriam_colin|title=In memoriam: Colin Rourke|publisher=Mathematics Institute at the University of Warwick|website=warwick.ac.uk|access-date=February 14, 2025}}</ref>

==Poincaré Conjecture==
In September 1986 Rourke and his graduate student, Eduardo Rêgo (later at [[University of Oporto]]), claimed to have solved the [[Poincaré Conjecture]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/09/30/science/one-of-math-s-major-problems-reported-solved.html?pagewanted=all|title=One of Math's Major Problems Reported Solved|author-link=James Gleick|first=James|last=Gleick|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=30 September 1986}}</ref> Reaction by the topological community at the time was highly skeptical, and during a special seminar at [[University of California, Berkeley]] given by Rourke, a fatal error was found in the proof.<ref name=szpiro>{{cite book|last=Szpiro|first=George G.|author-link=George Szpiro|title=Poincaré's Prize|url=https://archive.org/details/poincarsprizehun0000szpi/page/177|url-access=registration|year=2007|publisher=Dutton|pages=[https://archive.org/details/poincarsprizehun0000szpi/page/177 177&ndash;79]|isbn=978-0-525-95024-0}}</ref><ref name=oshea>{{cite book|last=O'Shea|first=Donal|author-link=Donal O'Shea|title=The Poincaré Conjecture|publisher=[[Walker Books]]|year=2007|pages=[https://archive.org/details/poincarconjectur0000oshe/page/179 179&ndash;80]|isbn=978-0-8027-1532-6|url=https://archive.org/details/poincarconjectur0000oshe/page/179}}</ref>

The part of the proof that was salvaged was a constructive characterization and enumeration of [[Heegaard splitting|Heegaard diagrams]] for [[homotopy sphere|homotopy 3-spheres]].<ref>{{cite journal|journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]]|author1-last=Rêgo|author1-first=Eduardo|author2-last=Rourke|author2-first=Colin|title=Heegaard diagrams and homotopy 3-spheres|volume=27|year=1988|issue=2|pages=137&ndash;43|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(88)90033-x|doi-access=}}</ref> A later-discovered algorithm of [[J. Hyam Rubinstein]] and [[Abigail Thompson]] identified when a homotopy 3-sphere was a topological 3-sphere.<ref>The proof later of the Poincaré Conjecture simplified this to "always yes".</ref>  Together, the two algorithms provided an algorithm that would find a counterexample to the Poincaré Conjecture, if one existed.<ref>{{cite journal|author-last=Rourke|author-first=Colin|title=Algorithms to disprove the Poincaré conjecture|journal=Turkish Journal of Mathematics|volume=21|year=1997|issue=1|pages=99&ndash;110}}</ref>

In 2002, [[Martin Dunwoody]] posted a claimed proof of the Poincaré Conjecture.<ref>{{cite web|title=A Proof of the Poincaré Conjecture ?|last=Dunwoody|first=M. J.|access-date=9 October 2015|url=http://www.personal.soton.ac.uk/mjd7/Poin.pdf}}</ref> Rourke identified its fatal flaw.<ref>{{cite news|title=Math whiz tackles old problem with new twist|newspaper=[[Sarasota Herald-Tribune]]|date=26 April 2002|page=6A|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1774&dat=20020426&id=yIIfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=0X8EAAAAIBAJ&pg=6867,135731&hl=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Szpiro|first=George G.|author-link=George Szpiro|title=Poincaré's Prize|url=https://archive.org/details/poincarsprizehun0000szpi/page/181|url-access=registration|year=2007|publisher=Dutton|pages=[https://archive.org/details/poincarsprizehun0000szpi/page/181 181&ndash;82]|isbn=978-0-525-95024-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=O'Shea|first=Donal|author-link=Donal O'Shea|title=The Poincaré Conjecture|publisher=Walker Books|year=2007|page=[https://archive.org/details/poincarconjectur0000oshe/page/187 187]|isbn=978-0-8027-1532-6|url=https://archive.org/details/poincarconjectur0000oshe/page/187}}</ref>

== Geometry & Topology ==
In 1996, dissatisfied with the rapidly rising fees charged by the major publishers of mathematical research journals, Rourke decided to start his own journal, and was assisted by [[Robion Kirby]], John Jones, and Brian Sanderson. The resulting journal, ''[[Geometry & Topology]]'', became a leading journal in its field. It was joined in 1998 by a proceedings and monographs series, ''Geometry & Topology Monographs'', and in 2000 by a sister journal, ''[[Algebraic & Geometric Topology]]''. Rourke wrote the software and managed these publications until around 2005 when he cofounded [[Mathematical Sciences Publishers]] (with Rob Kirby) to take over the running.

== Cosmology ==
In 2000, Rourke started taking an interest in [[cosmology]] and posted his first paper on the topic on the arXiv preprint server in 2003.  He collaborated with Robert MacKay, also of [[Warwick University]], with papers on [[redshift]], [[gamma-ray burst]]s and natural observer fields. He proposed a new paradigm for the universe, one that involves neither [[dark matter]] nor a [[Big Bang]]. This new paradigm was presented in "A new paradigm for the universe" (see bibliography).

The main idea is that the principal objects in the universe form a spectrum unified by the presence of a massive or hypermassive [[black hole]].  These objects are variously called [[quasar]]s, [[Active galactic nucleus|active galaxies]] and [[Spiral galaxy|spiral galaxies]].  The key to understanding their dynamics is [[angular momentum]] and the key tool is a proper formulation of "[[Mach's principle]]" using Sciama's ideas. This is added to standard [[general relativity]] in the form of hypothesized "inertial drag fields" which carry the forces that realize Mach's principle. This formulation solves the causal problems that occur in a naive formulation of the principle.

The new approach provides an explanation for the observed dynamics of spiral galaxies without needing [[dark matter]] and gives a framework that fits the observations of [[Halton Arp]] and others that show that [[quasar]]s typically exhibit [[Intrinsic redshift|instrinsic redshift]]. An accessible version was published by World Scientific in it its "Knots and everything" series no 71, titled "The geometry of the universe".
